items.title: Online False Positive Reduction via Statistical Process Controls
items.summary: Everyone seems to be obsessed with False Positives right now in Security. But this is a solved problem in other industries.. Some of them have data scientists that use Statsig , but all of them use some kind of a statistics engine that evaluates performance against costs and risk. How does a Hedge Fund choose to take the best performing prototype investment algorithms? They give them real data first, and then they use statistical analysis and optimize the results relative to the costs and risks involved, in order to screen for chosen models. What about running thousands of hypothesis tests across incoming data for disease prediction, then deciding which hypothesis tests discoveries to send to a team of experts to investigate? All of these have a few characteristics similar to the modern MSSP SOC. They run multiple hypothesis tests, continuously, across newly seen data. So each execution brings a unique test. The occurrence of True Positives is rare, so most findings are False Positives. They have fixed resource constraints limiting the number of investigations that the experts can complete, vs number of tests that can be patched/updated/engineered. So there are cost limits. The impact from missing True Positives is commercially high, so care is taken to quantify and measure risk . To any data scientist/statistician/economist/operations researcher.. a) how many expert-hours do we have? (SOCs can answer this) b) how big a queue can we clear? (SOCs can answer this) c) how much noise can we actually stomach? (SOC’s don’t know how to articulate this). d) how much risk of missed True Positives do we face? (This is why SOCs haven’t solved for cost minimization yet). So if this optimization problem has been solved in other areas (some with negative impacts being loss of life..) then why is it that SOCs keep saying they are drowning in False Postives? “The SOC is a screening operation running against a fixed budget of expert hours, but it treats itself as a unique problem child, because it has unmeasured uncertainty on how to manage it’s risk of missed True Positives.” — me calling it out. If your MSSP is chasing “FP reduction”, then it’s already failed to frame the problem correctly, and it will always have an optimization problem unsolved. You want to keep the noise inside a budget , for the least cost to business , without throwing away True Positives. But in order to do that we need to measure risk of lost True Positives.. So how do we do that? Lessons from the GUIDE Dataset A few years ago, Microsoft ran a competition on Kaggle , to help find data science solutions “that help security operations centers identify, prioritize, investigate, and respond to cybersecurity incidents”. They took a very large sample of incident data from their customer base, and provided it as the GUIDE dataset. GUIDE is the largest ground truth labelled incident dataset out there to date . It is composed of 707,000 graded incidents across 7,219 detectors and 5,340 tenants , every one labelled true-positive/benign-positive/false-positive, timestamped, and tagged with a MITRE ATT&CK tactic. For my analysis, I want to investigate what a MSSP with multiple customers looks like in the GUIDE dataset. So I focused on the 857 that generate incidents everyday over a 12 day period. This is because in my experience, if a SOC has a lot of FPs then it’s usual to see most of the daily incidents come from the same noisy customers or detectors. The dataset also validates this, but we’ll get there soon. Lesson 1: Class Definitions MATTER . GUIDE provides labels for incidents as True Positive, Benign Positive and False Positive. Those are the Microsoft labels, but many other tools use them too.. But someone with a bit of data science experience will challenge this.. Statistician — “hmmm? What is Benign Positive? Is that meant to be a class? Is this a multiclass confusion matrix ?” “Nono, it’s a security industry added gem! It means the test ran well, but the outcome wasn’t a True Positive! :)” — Security Industry Statistician — “em.. so it’s not a TP, so it’s a FP?” “Huh? its not a TP and not a FP dude” — Security Industry Statistician — “Where does BP sit in all of the time-tested statistical measures for classification performance?” “I don’t know. It’s built into my SIEM platforms.. so?” — Security Industry Statistician — “I mean, there’s some argument towards BP being a separate class, but it’s generally not used when we’re dealing with rare TP event discovery”. “So what do we do then? How would this impact our approach? — Security Industry” Let me show you. I believe that the industry has set itself up with a fundamental problem. Why does the SOC exist (outside of making profit)? It’s there to provide assurance to the customer that their environment is being protected from unwanted actions, detecting and remedying any that occur. That means that the class definitions should to be aligned to yield. When this is done, the definition of the ‘Benign Positive’ splits into two, one that belongs in true positive, and one that doesn’t. If you want to understand this more from a stats angle, you can read Fawcett, “An Introduction to ROC Analysis” or ask your favorite LLM.. So the real definitions at play are more like this (imo): True Positives a. [TP] Malicious / Unwanted Activity. Genuine threat or policy-violating activity, SOC cost to investigate is justified. This is why the SOC exists. b. [TP] Client Useful / Assurance. Not an attack, but the finding delivered value. E.g. misconfiguration, shadow IT, control failure. The cost justified. This is also why the SOC exists. False Positives a. [FP] Benign. No threat, no value delivered. Time spent, nothing returned to the customer. SOC incurs a cost, negative value to customer. It doesn’t matter if it’s a ‘suspicious process’ or a ‘anomalous X doing Y’, if it’s triaged and not within the two TP classes, then it’s a FP. b. [FP] Noise . No threat, no value delivered again.. Time spent triaging, and not even escalated to the customer or next analyst in escalation path. False Negatives d . [FN] Missed Malicious/Unwanted Activity . These are the genuine threat or policy-violating activties that your detection rules did not capture, that you later found out about. Penetration test reports, DFIR reports you review against, dare I say.. Real incidents? e. [FN] Missed incidents via rule review . These are the FNs found from reviewing your rulesets against the Detection Weakness Enumeration standard. True Negatives Most don’t bother defining this, but I tend to treat the size of the search space as as True Negatives, mostly because I’m sneaky and it makes you look less bad when you need the counts for your performance metrics. But you shouldn’t need to worry about it for the cost optimization problem in your SOC, because it’s somewhat useless for this. And if a customer needs a metric that needs the TN count, then you should provide it and provide them your confusion matrix too. Two things you might have noticed: The two TP determinations focus on maximizing value to the customer , aligned to the purpose of the SOC. This includes detections from penetration tests, in [TP] Client Useful / Assurance. . It’s the portion of the “Benign Positive” earlier that points to yield. The [FP] Benign class results in a cost to the customer, so it’s separate to the noise. This helps the SOC track it’s reduction. I included False Negatives. That’s because it’s a very real class that does actually exist. Are you tracking these??? Ok. Now that we have a definition of TP and FP, etc we will make all the Benign Positive labelled alerts in the GUIDE dataset False Positives, because that’s the risk adverse thing to do. Lesson 2: ‘Shit-In-Shit-Out’ is an unbiased universal law. When we investigate where the false positives come from, we see that appx 1% of detectors contribute around 80% of all FPs… The grey dotted line is the line of perfect equality, meaning that if all the detectors equally contributed to the volume of False Positives, then we’d see that line. The yellow vertical line shows a share of 10% (more later on this). When you see red and blue lines having a large prevalence of FPs, then we know that there are a few poorly designed detectors that are contributing the bulk of your FP pain. But what if they are caused by a few very noisy customers? Remember when I said I reduced the dataset down to those organizations that were active every single day of the 12 days? (reduced for my proposed stats engine, ‘always-on core as the mock MSSP customer base’). The above figure shows us that most of the incidents in the dataset were generated by organizations that produce incidents every day. But when we remove those organizations that only generated incidents once, we see that the skewedness of the noise to detectors doesn’t really change (below figure). But we know this already, why don’t we just cut them out? At 80% total FPs, the ~1% of detectors are the noisiest but are also the highest-volume, highest-recall rules. So a blunt “delete the noisy rules” cut removes ~all the noise loses 90% of true positives.. Lesson 3: True Positive Risk can be taken from GUIDE! ❤ When we look at the distribution of the gaps in time between each True Positive, we see that it’s very very dense at 1.3 minutes. This makes sense, attackers think in graphs, if we turned off a rule we’d probably still see some around it. The dataset shows us that TPs arrive in tight clusters and 98% of gaps are under 4 hours. But knowing that, what if once a detector is flagged for a patch, and it gets taken down, what RISK do we take on? What is the probability of MISSING a true positive incident while the detector is down? How does that change over time? If we park a rule forever (i.e cut it) then we lose 40% of all FUTURE TPs. But if we patch it within the first 4 hours, we’d only lose 1.3% of true positives. Within 1 hour is 0.3%, which is pretty low risk. As we delay the patch, the increasingly more likely it is that we’ll miss a True Positive incident. Hey, this means we have numbers to optimize against guys. But remember when we saw that detectors to FP volumes had a very strong skew? It turns out that at a 4 hour SLA to patch a flagged detector, 240 detectors of 331 flagged actually miss true positive incidents. So how do we use these lessons to solve the cost optimization problem? For this I propose Dynamic Incident Routing Engine or DIRE for short. Penalize the detectors that perform badly, do this continuously via betting e-values Route the flagged detectors based on their type of badness Do this informed by cost limitations for both patching and triage, and risk for missed TPs. Applying Dynamic Incident Routing Engine (DIRE) the Stats Engine I propose, to GUIDE. DIRE is a statistical process-control layer for the SOC. Just like the other industries have. It sits between the detection platforms and the SOC and only forwards incidents that statistically carry informative value. How it works There are two parts. First, the SOC Manager decides what thier tolerance for False Discovery Rate is. That’s FP/FP+TP. It tells you how much of the incidents can be tolerated as False Positive. For DIRE we model using 10%. 10% is pretty generous. The second part is the stats engine itself. Every hour, DIRE re-asks three questions of each rule: Q1: Are you globally bad? This detector’s noise rate vs all other detectors on the platform. If it’s shit across all customer environments, then it’s globally shit. Q2: bad for this customer? One tenant’s slice of the detector vs the same detector’s other tenants . If it’s only shit for a handful of customers, and not globally, then maybe the customer’s environment changed? Q3: spiking now? The last hour vs this rule’s own trailing baseline . Q1 and Q2 are lagging measures, if a detection rule suddenly flags the SOC, then it needs to be patched. DIRE measures evidence with an e-value . A detection rule is tested continuously, forever, on data that keeps growing. This means there is a “peeking” problem that invalidates p-values. E-values are built for exactly this reason. An e-value is actually a betting score . It’s how many times better the hypothesis “this rule is worse than its reference” predicted the data than “this rule is normal.” An e-value of 10 means 10-to-1 evidence. DIRE flags at e ≥ 1/α , and with α = 10% (the FDR tolerance rate mentioned above) that’s a 10:1 limit. Because “a fair bet against a true null can’t grow your money on average (E[e]=1)” a simple threshold gives a guaranteed ≤10% false discovery rate. That means you can scale up and down in your SOC modelling, and force your tolerance to be a constant. That has large implications in the commercial modelling benefits I’ll show later. DIRE creates a matrix (rows vs columns) of detectors vs customers, in order to asses whether customer environments have impacted the detector performance. A tenant with 5 false positives in 6 alerts isn’t “83% noise”, it’s unknown . Due to this DIRE shrinks every thin estimate toward the level above it (tenant-cell → detector → family → whole estate) using empirical-Bayes , after subtracting the sampling-noise component. Without this, tiny samples throw extreme rates that skew any ranking. Each rule is judged against a reference that excludes itself (leave-one-out sampling). Otherwise a bad rule ruins the baseline it’s being measured against. Q1 runs first, a globally-flagged detector skips its per-tenant tests as one MSSP-wide bad rule shouldn’t spawn fifty per-tenant tickets, and GUIDE data taught us that globally badness creates most of the FPs. And once anything is flagged it leaves both the queue and every future baseline, so one noisy rule can’t drag its neighbours’ references down with it. Every decision is auditable . Each step writes a ledger row per tenant-cell, counts, shrunk rate, the reference it was judged against, all three e-values, and the verdict. You can always answer “why was this flagged?”, or “why wasn’t it?”. DIRES output is a routable work-ticket with a costing. A flag emits a tuning task carrying the evidence, the reference rate, and a cross-tenant distribution, plus a 24-hour look-ahead risk score of lost TPs. It also outputs cost information: recurring analyst-hours, one-time engineer-hours, payback, and true-positives-at-risk. OK. So we’ve established that DIRE is a statistics engine that continuously bets on each detector based on it’s TP/FP performance, routs a work ticket, enables cost optimization, gives a business risk for the detector etc. For this example, I will apply DIRE to the 12 days in the GUIDE dataset. The following assumptions apply. The time to patch a globally bad detector is 16 hours. I think this is realistic, as it’s calendar time (not engineer time). A from scratch detector needs backtesting and emulation, so 16 hours is ok imo. The time to patch a locally bad detector is 4 hours. This means that the FPs coming in for the hour step for a detector:customer/organiztion flag as low informative value to the customer, so the SOC reviews FP notes and sees that there is an opportunity for a local exclusion/automation rule for the customer. 4 hours is enough time, the lag affect of DIRE means the FPs have SOC analyst notes included. The time windows above are based on the TP miss probabilities from GUIDE. DIRE needed 7 days of data to inform baselines, so the remaining 5 were the test window. First, RISK. How does DIRE perform over the 12 days with risk? When we consider that attackers think in graphs, and we would see other alerts inform a campaign, we can construct a risk score around campaigns. Yes, I used claude to help generate these figures. So what? When we considered a 16h and 4h patch windows, we lose 2.3% of campaigns. That was due to the large patch window sizes for globally bad rules. That reduces as we reduce the patch window. It may not be ideal, but it’s data we can incorporate into our planning in the SOC around how fast to patch, argue for resources for faster patching etc etc. The figure below shows us that the lost TPs are from the globally bad detectors, not quite from the local cell-level patches. That makes sense due to the skewedness of the FPs to the detectors. But this is risk from the GUIDE dataset, it doesn’t mean that a True Positive will occur. The figure below shows us where these risks occur in the MITRE ATT&CK tactic level. The bulk of this risk is initial access based, so if customers enforce strong Conditional Access policies and App Policies (if entra) and phishing resistant 2FA, the risk has a mitigation to help support the larger patch window. In fact, from the DIRE simulation we can see that 71% of the risk is introduced by the top 10 volumous detectors. That further supports the need to emulate your highest performing detectors if they are also very noisy. You’ll notice that, these risks are much lower than if we were to straight cut the detectors out. That’s because we DIRE’s patch windows allow for time to better emulate detectors and catch TPs. So now we know the risks, the next question to ask is the benefit that taking the risk leads to, and what the costs are that offset the benefit. Finding 2, Continuous FP reduction benefit. In DIRE we assume that an incident takes 20 minutes to triage. We assume that every patch requires an engineer time. Although we don’t provide the analysis in a dollar value, but a time unit, it wouldn’t be difficult for a SOC manager to take DIRE outputs and apply them to a cost model. The figure above shows us that once DIRE starts flagging incidents for patching, running tests each hour, that the prevalence engine (Q1–3) drop false positives from 82% to 59%, with the FDR tolerance limit further dropping it to 22%, closer to the 10% budget. We don’t see the 10% being meet post 15th June, but if we had more data we would have seen it trend downward as it’s a lag model. The gradual reduction post the immediate drop shows that the top worse performing detectors that skew the FP volumes get flagged almost immediately, with consecutive reductions occurring due to the prevalence tracker (the e-values). Fixing the top 10 flagged detectors recovers in benefits 60% all avaliable recoverable cost. That means that a short burst of engineering effort solves most of the pain issues. We kind of knew that already though right? Glad the data shows us this. These hundreds of hours represents the volume of detectors that GUIDE dataset has, so in practice it’s likely even smaller. When we consider the engineering cost as a one off for a detector, and the savings to be reocurrong we see that one we factor in the risks from GUIDE data, the benefit is huge. We just needed to know the risk. The figure below shows us that as long as the TP risk has mitigations (discussed above) prior to patch, then there is little argument to keep a detector running prior to a patch starting. In fact, when comparing an identify and cut approach to DIRE, we find that DIRE removes 96% of all False Positives (of cut rules), and only lost 5% of the True Positives in the GUIDE data (because they happened to occur within the patch windows). And if we really can’t tolerate that much risk, even post mitigation steps, then we can directly reduce it by shortening the patch window for globally bad detectors, which are the contributors to the risk, as demonstrated below on the left (flagged cells are the detector vs organization pairs). The return efficiency is pretty good. If we can accept the risk, then we should implement DIRE. Finding 3, Patch TODO ticket routing and SOC scalability DIRE’s two step method of FDR tolerance and evalue show that the long term benefits/savings of DIRE can be found in the local patches within customer environments with 25% local savings from the FDR tolerance of 10% and 16% from the evalue tracking. When a SOC has an environment that is tuned, and platform teams can attribute SOC savings to revenue, and there are SLAs on the types of patching that DIRE raises, then we see an almost uniform saving of 80% all FPs over each SOC shift, where actually the evening shift sees more of the residual queue than the day shift. This isn’t surprising, as we saw earlier that most of the FPs peaked during business hours. Once this level of control, performance evaluation can be achieved in a SOC, then it is easier to scale up and down and know the cost impacts. Final Remarks The SOC isn’t a unique problem child. It’s a screening operation, thousands of continuous tests, rare true positives, a fixed budget of expert hours, a high cost for anything missed. Other industries solved this by measuring the cost of the noise against the risk of the miss . Security chased “FP reduction” instead, which is a target with no risk articulated, so set your eyes on optimising to risk. GUIDE data gives us a prior for risk. TPs arrive in tight clusters, so the cost of parking a detector is function you can read off the data. 40% of future TPs if you cut it forever, 1.3% if you patch inside 4 hours, 0.3% inside one hour. DIRE is just the stats engine that spends the cost deliberately to get 96% of the FPs of a naive cut, at 5% of the TP loss. That’s an informed case for any for-profit-SOC. Source code coming soon. Online False Positive Reduction via Statistical Process Controls was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

The second part is the stats engine itself.

Every hour, DIRE re-asks three questions of each rule:

  • Q1: Are you globally bad? This detector’s noise rate vs all other detectors on the platform. If it’s shit across all customer environments, then it’s globally shit.
  • Q2: bad for this customer? One tenant’s slice of the detector vs the same detector’s other tenants. If it’s only shit for a handful of customers, and not globally, then maybe the customer’s environment changed?
  • Q3: spiking now? The last hour vs this rule’s own trailing baseline. Q1 and Q2 are lagging measures, if a detection rule suddenly flags the SOC, then it needs to be patched.

DIRE measures evidence with an e-value. A detection rule is tested continuously, forever, on data that keeps growing. This means there is a “peeking” problem that invalidates p-values. E-values are built for exactly this reason.

An e-value is actually a betting score. It’s how many times better the hypothesis “this rule is worse than its reference” predicted the data than “this rule is normal.” An e-value of 10 means 10-to-1 evidence. DIRE flags at e ≥ 1/α, and with α = 10% (the FDR tolerance rate mentioned above) that’s a 10:1 limit. Because “a fair bet against a true null can’t grow your money on average (E[e]=1)” a simple threshold gives a guaranteed ≤10% false discovery rate. That means you can scale up and down in your SOC modelling, and force your tolerance to be a constant. That has large implications in the commercial modelling benefits I’ll show later.

DIRE creates a matrix (rows vs columns) of detectors vs customers, in order to asses whether customer environments have impacted the detector performance.

  • A tenant with 5 false positives in 6 alerts isn’t “83% noise”, it’s unknown. Due to this DIRE shrinks every thin estimate toward the level above it (tenant-cell → detector → family → whole estate) using empirical-Bayes, after subtracting the sampling-noise component. Without this, tiny samples throw extreme rates that skew any ranking.
  • Each rule is judged against a reference that excludes itself (leave-one-out sampling). Otherwise a bad rule ruins the baseline it’s being measured against.
  • Q1 runs first, a globally-flagged detector skips its per-tenant tests as one MSSP-wide bad rule shouldn’t spawn fifty per-tenant tickets, and GUIDE data taught us that globally badness creates most of the FPs. And once anything is flagged it leaves both the queue and every future baseline, so one noisy rule can’t drag its neighbours’ references down with it.
  • Every decision is auditable. Each step writes a ledger row per tenant-cell, counts, shrunk rate, the reference it was judged against, all three e-values, and the verdict. You can always answer “why was this flagged?”, or “why wasn’t it?”.

DIRES output is a routable work-ticket with a costing. A flag emits a tuning task carrying the evidence, the reference rate, and a cross-tenant distribution, plus a 24-hour look-ahead risk score of lost TPs. It also outputs cost information: recurring analyst-hours, one-time engineer-hours, payback, and true-positives-at-risk.

OK. So we’ve established that DIRE is a statistics engine that continuously bets on each detector based on it’s TP/FP performance, routs a work ticket, enables cost optimization, gives a business risk for the detector etc.

For this example, I will apply DIRE to the 12 days in the GUIDE dataset. The following assumptions apply.

  • The time to patch a globally bad detector is 16 hours. I think this is realistic, as it’s calendar time (not engineer time). A from scratch detector needs backtesting and emulation, so 16 hours is ok imo.
  • The time to patch a locally bad detector is 4 hours. This means that the FPs coming in for the hour step for a detector:customer/organiztion flag as low informative value to the customer, so the SOC reviews FP notes and sees that there is an opportunity for a local exclusion/automation rule for the customer. 4 hours is enough time, the lag affect of DIRE means the FPs have SOC analyst notes included.
  • The time windows above are based on the TP miss probabilities from GUIDE.
  • DIRE needed 7 days of data to inform baselines, so the remaining 5 were the test window.

First, RISK. How does DIRE perform over the 12 days with risk?

When we consider that attackers think in graphs, and we would see other alerts inform a campaign, we can construct a risk score around campaigns.

Yes, I used claude to help generate these figures. So what?

When we considered a 16h and 4h patch windows, we lose 2.3% of campaigns. That was due to the large patch window sizes for globally bad rules. That reduces as we reduce the patch window. It may not be ideal, but it’s data we can incorporate into our planning in the SOC around how fast to patch, argue for resources for faster patching etc etc.

The figure below shows us that the lost TPs are from the globally bad detectors, not quite from the local cell-level patches. That makes sense due to the skewedness of the FPs to the detectors.

But this is risk from the GUIDE dataset, it doesn’t mean that a True Positive will occur. The figure below shows us where these risks occur in the MITRE ATT&CK tactic level. The bulk of this risk is initial access based, so if customers enforce strong Conditional Access policies and App Policies (if entra) and phishing resistant 2FA, the risk has a mitigation to help support the larger patch window.

In fact, from the DIRE simulation we can see that 71% of the risk is introduced by the top 10 volumous detectors. That further supports the need to emulate your highest performing detectors if they are also very noisy. You’ll notice that, these risks are much lower than if we were to straight cut the detectors out. That’s because we DIRE’s patch windows allow for time to better emulate detectors and catch TPs.

So now we know the risks, the next question to ask is the benefit that taking the risk leads to, and what the costs are that offset the benefit.

Finding 2, Continuous FP reduction benefit.

In DIRE we assume that an incident takes 20 minutes to triage. We assume that every patch requires an engineer time. Although we don’t provide the analysis in a dollar value, but a time unit, it wouldn’t be difficult for a SOC manager to take DIRE outputs and apply them to a cost model.

The figure above shows us that once DIRE starts flagging incidents for patching, running tests each hour, that the prevalence engine (Q1–3) drop false positives from 82% to 59%, with the FDR tolerance limit further dropping it to 22%, closer to the 10% budget. We don’t see the 10% being meet post 15th June, but if we had more data we would have seen it trend downward as it’s a lag model.

The gradual reduction post the immediate drop shows that the top worse performing detectors that skew the FP volumes get flagged almost immediately, with consecutive reductions occurring due to the prevalence tracker (the e-values).

Fixing the top 10 flagged detectors recovers in benefits 60% all avaliable recoverable cost. That means that a short burst of engineering effort solves most of the pain issues. We kind of knew that already though right? Glad the data shows us this.

These hundreds of hours represents the volume of detectors that GUIDE dataset has, so in practice it’s likely even smaller.

When we consider the engineering cost as a one off for a detector, and the savings to be reocurrong we see that one we factor in the risks from GUIDE data, the benefit is huge. We just needed to know the risk. The figure below shows us that as long as the TP risk has mitigations (discussed above) prior to patch, then there is little argument to keep a detector running prior to a patch starting.

In fact, when comparing an identify and cut approach to DIRE, we find that DIRE removes 96% of all False Positives (of cut rules), and only lost 5% of the True Positives in the GUIDE data (because they happened to occur within the patch windows).

And if we really can’t tolerate that much risk, even post mitigation steps, then we can directly reduce it by shortening the patch window for globally bad detectors, which are the contributors to the risk, as demonstrated below on the left (flagged cells are the detector vs organization pairs).

The return efficiency is pretty good. If we can accept the risk, then we should implement DIRE.

Finding 3, Patch TODO ticket routing and SOC scalability

DIRE’s two step method of FDR tolerance and evalue show that the long term benefits/savings of DIRE can be found in the local patches within customer environments with 25% local savings from the FDR tolerance of 10% and 16% from the evalue tracking.

When a SOC has an environment that is tuned, and platform teams can attribute SOC savings to revenue, and there are SLAs on the types of patching that DIRE raises, then we see an almost uniform saving of 80% all FPs over each SOC shift, where actually the evening shift sees more of the residual queue than the day shift. This isn’t surprising, as we saw earlier that most of the FPs peaked during business hours.

Once this level of control, performance evaluation can be achieved in a SOC, then it is easier to scale up and down and know the cost impacts.

Final Remarks

The SOC isn’t a unique problem child. It’s a screening operation, thousands of continuous tests, rare true positives, a fixed budget of expert hours, a high cost for anything missed.

Other industries solved this by measuring the cost of the noise against the risk of the miss. Security chased “FP reduction” instead, which is a target with no risk articulated, so set your eyes on optimising to risk.

GUIDE data gives us a prior for risk. TPs arrive in tight clusters, so the cost of parking a detector is function you can read off the data. 40% of future TPs if you cut it forever, 1.3% if you patch inside 4 hours, 0.3% inside one hour.

DIRE is just the stats engine that spends the cost deliberately to get 96% of the FPs of a naive cut, at 5% of the TP loss. That’s an informed case for any for-profit-SOC.

items.title: AWS Network Firewall Now Displays Count of Triggered Security Rules
items.summary: AWS has introduced rule hit count support for AWS Network Firewall , giving security teams direct visibility into which stateful firewall rules are matching live network traffic. The new capability is enabled by default and helps organizations identify active, inactive, and potentially misconfigured rules without manually reviewing large volumes of firewall logs. As firewall policies grow, they often accumulate rules that are no longer needed, never trigger, or are placed incorrectly in the inspection order. Until now, teams had to search alert logs manually to determine whether a specific rule was being used. This could make firewall cleanup, incident investigations, and compliance validation slow and difficult. The rule hit count feature uses AWS Network Firewall alert logs to show how frequently individual stateful rules match traffic. AWS Network Firewall Shows Triggered Security Rules The AWS console’s Top Rule Hits dashboard displays the signature ID, rule description, resource ARN, total hit count, percentage of overall hits, and the most recent time the rule was triggered. This lets security teams quickly determine whether a control is active. A rule that repeatedly appears in the dashboard is matching traffic, while a rule that does not appear during the selected lookback period may be unused, outdated, or positioned behind another matching rule. Rule hit count from the dashboard (source: AWS) AWS Network Firewall counts a rule hit only when the traffic match generates an alert log. Rules using alert, drop, or reject actions are included because these actions create alert records. However, pass rules do not create alert logs by default and therefore do not appear in hit count data. Organizations that want to measure matches for allow rules can add the alert keyword to a Suricata pass rule. For example, a rule can permit HTTPS traffic while simultaneously creating an alert log. This allows teams to monitor authorized traffic patterns without blocking the connection. AWS adds an aws_metadata field to alert logs, including the ARN of the rule group or firewall policy that produced the event. Analysts can combine the resource ARN with the Suricata signature ID (SID) to identify the exact rule that generated an alert, with alert data delivered to Amazon CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3. Security operations teams can investigate the logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights or Amazon Athena, while the native Network Firewall monitoring dashboard provides an easier view of the most frequently triggered rules. The feature can help during incident response. For example, if a security team suspects outbound communication with a malicious domain, it can filter the rule hit count view to the relevant time period. This can reveal whether a domain-blocking or threat-detection rule triggered , how often it matched, and when the most recent event occurred. Rule hit counts can also support compliance operations. Teams working with PCI DSS 4.0, DORA, and internal governance requirements can use the data as evidence that firewall controls are functioning. It also helps central cloud security teams review policies managed for multiple business units and remove dormant rules that consume capacity without adding protection. AWS noted that system-generated signature IDs may also appear in the dashboard. These can represent strict-order default actions, such as dropping established traffic that did not match an explicit rule. In these cases, the displayed ARN points to the firewall policy rather than a stateful rule group. Rule hit count is available at no additional AWS Network Firewall charge, although normal CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, and Athena storage or query fees still apply. The capability supports stateful rules only; stateless rules are not currently covered. It is available in supported AWS Regions except the Middle East Bahrain and Middle East UAE Regions. Prevent incidents due to slow investigations. items.title: Malicious npm Packages Deploy AI-Powered RedC2 Linux Implant to Steal Credentials and Pivot Networks
items.summary: Malicious npm packages are being used to place a Linux backdoor inside calendar and streak-calculation tools. The packages deliver legitimate date functions, making the malicious code easy to miss. The danger begins when an affected module is imported. The loader makes a bundled Linux program executable and starts it in the background, without an install script or suspicious function call. TrendAI researchers identified the campaign as a software supply chain attack that delivers RedShell, the Linux implant associated with the RedC2 command-and-control framework. TrendAI said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that it shows how a harmless-looking dependency can become an entry point into a production environment. The impact extends beyond the initial host. The implant can collect credentials, explore a network, move traffic through an infected machine and pull in extra tools. That puts source code, cloud access and internal services at risk when a poisoned package reaches a trusted build chain. Malicious npm Packages Deploy AI-Powered RedC2 Linux Implant The affected packages pose as small, dependency-free utilities for date math. Their advertised features work as expected, while a hidden binary is presented as a native helper. This blend of useful code and concealed execution is why malicious npm package campaigns remain difficult for teams to spot early. The entry file, dist/index.mjs , runs automatically as the module loads. It checks for the binary, changes its permissions and verifies its SHA-256 value before starting it as a detached process. RedC2 advertisement (Source – TrendAI) Since it does not rely on lifecycle hooks, using --ignore-scripts does not stop this route to execution. A direct or transitive import can trigger the implant, even if the developer never selected the package. Similar techniques have shown how configuration file supply chain attacks can sidestep controls built around familiar npm lifecycle scripts. The binary is RedShell, a native Linux component introduced in RedC2 4.0. The implant uses separate plain HTTP paths for data theft and payload downloads. RedC2 dashboard (Source – TrendAI) The report describes RedShell as capable of taking SSH keys, browser-stored credentials and database-related files. It can create persistence through cron, shell startup files, user-level services or desktop autostart entries. These actions can give intruders a durable foothold after the original package has been removed. AI Assistance Raises the Stakes RedC2 includes Red Agent, a feature that turns a plain-language request into a sequence of commands for an infected system. An operator can ask for reconnaissance or credential collection rather than manually issuing every step. The AI layer can make follow-on activity faster and easier to coordinate. RedShell can run commands, open a reverse shell, transfer files and inspect users, processes and network settings. It supports SOCKS5 proxying, TCP port forwarding and tunnelling, features that can turn one compromised Linux host into a bridge toward otherwise unreachable systems. The risk resembles recent CI credential theft incidents in which developer environments provided valuable access beyond one workstation. Security teams should check lockfiles, package caches and build artifacts for the affected package names and versions. RedShell execution flow (Source – TrendAI) Any host that imported one should be treated as potentially compromised: isolate it, rotate exposed credentials, inspect persistence locations and review outbound connections. Removing a dependency alone may not remove a launched implant or undo stolen secrets. Defenders should watch for Node processes changing bundled .bin files to executable, unexpected background children from dependency directories, and traffic to the listed addresses and ports. Tightening dependency approval, pinning versions, reviewing package contents and limiting build-system permissions reduce the blast radius. The case reinforces lessons from cross-platform malware delivery attacks where native payloads hide behind trusted development tools. For incident response, prioritize hosts with access to source repositories, deployment keys, cloud tokens or production networks. Search endpoint telemetry for the RedShell hash and filenames, block confirmed malicious communications where appropriate, and preserve logs before rebuilding systems. The evidence points to a threat designed to establish a route for network compromise. items.title: Critical isolated-vm Flaw Lets Untrusted JavaScript Escape Sandbox and Hijack Host Execution
items.summary: A critical security flaw in the popular Node.js sandboxing library isolated-vm could allow untrusted JavaScript to escape its V8 sandbox and potentially hijack execution in the host process. The issue, tracked as GHSA-864f-rcv7-6rh4 and awaiting a CVE identifier, affects isolated-vm versions earlier than 7.0.1 and 6.2.0. The maintainers released fixes on August 8, 2026. The vulnerability exists in ExternalCopy, a feature used by isolated-vm to move data between separate V8 Isolates. V8 Isolates are designed to separate JavaScript environments by giving each sandbox its own heap, built-in objects, and object graph. This prevents sandboxed code from directly accessing host objects unless the host intentionally exposes a capability, such as an ivm.Reference. Endorlabs researchers found that the V8 isolation primitive itself was not broken. Instead, the flaw was located in native C++ binding code responsible for transferring data across the isolation boundary. The issue involves the transferList option used by ExternalCopy. This option allows ArrayBuffer memory to be transferred rather than copied, improving performance for large buffers. During processing, the affected code iterates over the transfer list twice. The first iteration verifies that every entry is an ArrayBuffer. The second iteration transfers the same entries but does not revalidate their types. Critical isolated-vm Flaw An attacker can exploit this gap through a JavaScript getter. During the first read, the getter returns a valid ArrayBuffer, allowing validation to succeed. During the second read, it returns a different value, such as an integer or string. The native code then treats that unexpected value as an ArrayBuffer through an unchecked conversion. This creates a type-confusion flaw and a time-of-check/time-of-use, or TOCTOU, condition. The host process can then dereference attacker-controlled memory-like data, causing a crash. ExternalCopy vulnerability works (source: Endor Labs) According to Endor Labs researchers , this flaw can be escalated beyond denial-of-service attacks to hijack the host process’s control flow. The attack can be triggered from inside a sandbox with only one exposed IVM.Reference. That is important because references are commonly used to provide limited functionality to sandboxed scripts. By retrieving the ExternalCopy constructor through an exposed reference, an attacker can build the malicious transfer list entirely from within the isolated environment. The minimum impact is a crash of a reliable host process, creating a denial-of-service condition . The maximum demonstrated impact is control-flow hijacking in the host process, which could lead to arbitrary code execution outside the sandbox. The risk is significant for multi-tenant applications, AI agent platforms, workflow automation tools, user-script runners, and services that execute customer-provided JavaScript. Products that use isolated-vm to isolate automation scripts or model-generated code should review their deployments immediately. The maintainers fixed the issue by preventing JavaScript execution while ExternalCopy performs the sensitive copy operation. This blocks getters, proxies, and similar mechanisms from changing values between validation and transfer. Organizations should upgrade to isolated-vm 7.0.1 or 6.2.0 as soon as possible. Security teams should also reduce the capabilities shared with sandboxed code and audit native binding layers, because a strong isolation primitive can still be undermined by unsafe glue code around it. items.title: Cybermes – AI Red Teaming Agent for Automated Penetration Testing
items.summary: A new open-source project called Cybermes has entered the crowded field of AI-powered offensive security tooling, positioning itself as an enterprise-grade autonomous agent capable of running full penetration tests with minimal human oversight. Released by developer Zyrexnn and hosted on GitHub , Cybermes now sits at version 2.0.0 following a major architectural overhaul that shifted its performance-critical components from Python to native Go binaries. The tool has been described publicly as an “Autonomous Offensive Security, Bug Bounty & Red Teaming Agent Framework” built around what its creators call the Hermes reasoning engine. At its core, Cybermes automates the reconnaissance-to-reporting pipeline that human penetration testers traditionally handle manually. The agent performs attack surface discovery, authenticated vulnerability research, and exploit validation, then compiles its findings into polished executive reports without requiring an analyst to stitch results together by hand. Cybermes – AI Red Teaming Agent This mirrors a broader industry trend toward agentic AI red teaming, exemplified by Microsoft’s own AI Red Teaming Agent inside Azure AI Foundry, which likewise automates adversarial testing and generates attack success rate scorecards for generative AI systems. Cybermes, however, targets traditional web applications and infrastructure rather than large language model safety testing, drawing on more than 50 bundled security skills covering IDOR and BOLA testing, authentication bypass playbooks, race condition detection, and injection matrices for SSRF and DOM-based XSS. One of the more notable claims surrounding Cybermes is its “zero-false-positive gate,” a validation layer that reportedly requires deterministic HTTP proof, exact status codes, and a standalone reproducible Python proof-of-concept script before any finding is written into a report. This design directly addresses a chronic pain point in automated scanning tools, which frequently flood analysts with unverified or speculative alerts that waste triage time. To make this feasible at scale, the tool relies on a token-economy architecture: a native Go component called smart_pipe intercepts noisy terminal output from reconnaissance tools like katana and ffuf, filters out static asset clutter and 404 noise, and streams only high-signal results to the underlying reasoning model, reportedly cutting token consumption by 70 to 85 percent per scanning phase. Once an assessment concludes, Cybermes automatically produces four deliverables in parallel: a markdown executive summary, a structured JSON metadata file for CI/CD pipelines , an interactive HTML dashboard, and a print-ready PDF report complete with CVSS v3.1 scorecards and color-coded risk badges. The underlying toolchain wires together well-known open-source utilities including subfinder, httpx, nmap, nuclei, sqlmap, and dalfox, alongside a 48-pattern credential scanner and an offline knowledge base built from resources like PayloadsAllTheThings and HackTricks. This kind of orchestration layer reflects a growing pattern across the AI red-teaming ecosystem on GitHub, where dozens of projects now bundle agent scan, MCP scan , and jailbreak evaluation capabilities into unified platforms. Cybermes supports installation on Linux, macOS, Windows via PowerShell or WSL2, and Docker, with a Telegram bot gateway allowing operators to trigger assessments remotely. Cybermes installation Notably, the project is distributed under the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0, meaning commercial use is restricted, and its documentation explicitly requires that all testing occur only against authorized targets under a structured “Scope and Authorization” framing. Security teams evaluating Cybermes should treat its zero-false-positive and reporting claims as vendor-stated until independently benchmarked, a caveat that applies broadly to the fast-moving category of autonomous AI red teaming tools now emerging alongside enterprise offerings from Microsoft and other major vendors. items.title: New Malware-as-a-service Leveraging Adobe-themed Domain to Attack Windows Users Using .bat File
items.summary: A criminal service is hiding behind a website that appears to offer Adobe Acrobat Reader. The site, acrobatreaderonline.com, is not a document service. Instead, it appears to expose an operator panel for building and managing attacks against Windows users. The campaign uses a familiar trick: a trusted-looking document or payment theme leads a target toward a harmful download. Earlier activity tied to the same infrastructure used a Windows batch, or .bat, file through a WebDAV remote folder, turning a PDF or boleto lure into a possible malware entry point. Researchers at Clandestine identified the operation during an open-source review on August 23, finding a live malware-as-a-service, or MaaS, panel behind the Adobe-themed domain. Clandestine said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that the site was not an Adobe reader portal and should not be treated as safe. https://t.co/LaGothWxgV is not Adobe Acrobat Reader Online. Open-source review on 23 August 2026 shows a live malware-as-a-service panel behind an Adobe-themed domain. The page title is SecureWorkspace WebPanel; /api/ renders as Kaido Panel. The stack is Vite/React, Tailwind… pic.twitter.com/arJGRFqXto — Clandestine (@akaclandestine) August 23, 2026 The discovery shows how a convincing brand imitation can move from a phishing lure to a working criminal platform. It contains features for collecting victim data, managing files and preparing malware modules, lowering the barrier for operators. New Malware-as-a-service Leveraging Adobe-themed Domain The domain creates a serious trust problem for people searching for a PDF reader, opening document links or responding to payment messages. Its public page uses the title “SecureWorkspace WebPanel,” while an application route identifies itself as “Kaido Panel.” Neither is a legitimate document viewer or cloud document service. Behind the landing page, researchers found protected endpoints for a command-and-control interface and a live SignalR communication hub. Unauthenticated requests returned a bearer-authentication challenge, showing the site is more than a static decoy. It is designed to give authorized operators access to backend functions. Public JavaScript exposed references to a builder, file manager, authentication refresh function and a section labelled loot. The code listed modules connected with information theft, banking overlays, PIX payments and boleto lures. That mix makes the operation relevant to Windows users and organizations processing financial documents. The documented delivery chain shows why a file extension can matter as much as a document name. Historical sandbox records linked Kaido infrastructure to a WebDAV loader using a .bat dropper and the Windows WebClient service. Similar Windows File Explorer WebDAV abuse can open remote content in ways that appear less suspicious than a conventional download. A batch file can run commands when a victim opens it, so it should never be assumed to be a harmless document. Users should question supposed PDF files with unusual extensions, shortcuts or download prompts. Recent fake Adobe document campaigns have likewise used familiar sharing language to persuade recipients to run unwanted software. Infrastructure and Defensive Actions The domain was registered in June 2026 and uses Cloudflare-hosted infrastructure. Its nameservers match those used by kaido.sh, a related domain seen earlier. At the time of review, only the www host resolved; several likely service names did not. A future address assigned to those names may signal a command-and-control shift. This justifies immediate checks. Organizations should block the identified domains across DNS, web proxies and email controls, then examine logs for requests to them. Teams should look for unexpected WebClient activity and the listed local cache artifact, which can reveal WebDAV-based delivery. Users should download Acrobat Reader only from Adobe’s official domain, not lookalike sites or unsolicited links. Security teams should avoid logging into the panel or executing files obtained from it. The risk fits a pattern seen in malware disguised as trusted apps , where recognizable names weaken a user’s caution. For defenders, combine domain blocking with alerts for suspicious remote-folder connections and script launches. Preserve relevant telemetry before action, check whether artifacts appear on endpoints, and report the infrastructure to the registrar, hosting provider and national response teams. A Windows AllaKore malware operation illustrates how PDF lures, WebDAV and batch scripts can form a multi-stage Windows compromise. There are some edge cases I want to validate the impact of, namely the inability to keep the door both closed and unlocked, and some of the assumptions I've made around access methods. The laundry will be our low-impact test case; then, if that's all good, I'll start rolling this approach out much more seriously across the house. Stay tuned, I think this will actually be pretty awesome.
